articles.title: How to Clear IGN Notes at Stanley Mosk Courthouse
articles.text: If you're handling a probate case in Los Angeles County, you'll inevitably encounter IGN notes—the probate examiner's flags that can derail your hearing and add months to your case. This guide explains exactly what they are and how to clear them.What Are IGN Notes?IGN stands for Incomplete, Grant, or Needs. These are notes posted by probate examiners at the Stanley Mosk Courthouse approximately 5-10 days before your scheduled probate hearing.The Los Angeles Superior Court centralizes all probate cases at Stanley Mosk, handling thousands of cases annually. To manage this volume, specialized probate examiners review every filing before the judge sees it. If they find any issues—even minor ones—they post notes.Critical WarningIf you appear at your hearing with uncleared IGN notes, the judge will continue your case—typically for another 3+ months. This is one of the most common causes of probate delays in LA County.Common Reasons for IGN NotesBased on our experience with hundreds of cases, these are the most common issues that trigger examiner notes:1Missing heir information - Names, addresses, or relationships not properly stated2Bond calculation errors - Incorrect total or missing bond waiver documentation3Inconsistent dates or names - Typos or variations between documents4Missing proof of mailing - DE-121 not properly completed or filed5Publication issues - Newspaper not adjudicated or dates incorrect6Will attachment problems - Original not submitted or copy not certifiedThe 5-Step Process to Clear IGN Notes1Access the Court PortalLog into the LA Superior Court website 5-10 days before your scheduled hearing. Navigate to your case and check for any posted examiner notes.2Review Each Note CarefullyRead every note in detail. Each one specifies exactly what information is missing or what correction is needed. Don't skip any—all must be addressed.3Draft Your Verified SupplementPrepare a formal "Supplement to the Petition" that specifically addresses each deficiency. This must be a verified document (signed under penalty of perjury).4Attorney ReviewHave the supplement reviewed by a licensed California probate attorney to ensure it properly addresses all issues and is formatted correctly for the court.5File Before Your HearingFile the verified supplement at least 2 court days before your hearing. This gives the examiner time to review and clear the notes from your file.What is a Verified Supplement?A Verified Supplement is a formal court document that corrects or adds information to your original Petition for Probate. It must:Reference your case number and the original petitionSpecifically address each examiner noteBe signed under penalty of perjuryInclude any supporting documentation referencedWhy DIY Supplements Often FailMany self-represented executors try to draft their own supplements, but they often fail because:They don't understand the legal terminology used in the notesThey address symptoms rather than root causesThey use incorrect formatting or miss verification requirementsThey file too late for the examiner to review before the hearingHow MyProbateCA Handles IGN NotesOur flat $3,995 fee includes complete IGN note clearance. This guide breaks down the statutory fee structure and shows you how to save $15,000-$25,000+ on your case.What Are Statutory Fees?California Probate Code Section 10810 sets the "statutory" fee schedule that attorneys can charge for probate work. This fee is calculated as a percentage of the gross estate value:Estate ValueFee PercentageFirst $100,0004%Next $100,0003%Next $800,0002%Next $9,000,0001%Above $10,000,0000.5%The Gross Value ProblemHere's what catches most people off guard: statutory fees are calculated on gross value, not net equity. articles.title: What is a Probate Referee in California?
articles.text: Every California probate case requires working with a Probate Referee—a court-appointed official who appraises estate assets. This guide explains who they are, what they do, and how to work with them effectively.What is a Probate Referee?A Probate Referee is a specially qualified appraiser appointed by the California State Controller to value estate assets for probate proceedings. They're not employees of the court—they're independent professionals licensed to provide official valuations.When you file a Petition for Probate, the court automatically assigns a Probate Referee to your case. You don't choose them—they're assigned on a rotating basis in each county.Key Facts About Probate RefereesAppointmentCourt-AssignedYou don't chooseFee0.1% of assets$75 minimumDeadline4 monthsFrom LettersWhat Does a Probate Referee Appraise?The Probate Referee values all non-cash assets in the estate. This includes:Real estate - Homes, land, commercial property, rental propertiesVehicles - Cars, boats, RVs, motorcyclesSecurities - Stocks, bonds, mutual funds (valued at date of death)Business interests - Ownership in LLCs, partnerships, corporationsPersonal property - Jewelry, art, collectibles, furnitureWhat the Executor ValuesThe executor (not the referee) values cash and cash equivalents: bank accounts, money market accounts, and similar liquid assets. You report these values on the Inventory & Appraisal form.Probate Referee FeesThe Probate Referee charges 0.1% (one-tenth of one percent) of the total assets they appraise, with a minimum fee of $75. This fee is paid from estate funds.Assets AppraisedReferee Fee (0.1%)$100,000$100$500,000$500$1,000,000$1,000$2,000,000$2,000The Inventory & Appraisal ProcessHere's how the process works:1Receive Letters TestamentaryThe 4-month clock for the Inventory & Appraisal starts when you receive your Letters.2Compile Asset ListIdentify all assets that need appraisal and gather supporting documentation (deeds, statements, titles).3Contact the Probate RefereeReach out to the assigned referee with your asset list. They may schedule property inspections if needed.4Receive AppraisalThe referee provides their official valuations, which you incorporate into Form DE-160.5File the Inventory & AppraisalSubmit Form DE-160 to the court within the 4-month deadline, signed by you and the referee.Tips for Working with Probate RefereesStart early - Don't wait until month 3 to contact the refereeBe organized - Provide complete documentation for each assetRespond promptly - Answer the referee's questions quicklyAllow access - If they need to inspect property, schedule it promptlyHow MyProbateCA HelpsOur $3,995 flat fee includes full coordination with the Probate Referee:We identify which assets need referee appraisalWe prepare and organize all documentationWe communicate with the referee on your behalfWe prepare and file Form DE-160 correctlyNeed help with the Inventory & Appraisal process? articles.title: Letters Testamentary California: Your Golden Ticket Explained
articles.text: Letters Testamentary are the single most important document you'll receive as an executor. Without them, you can't access bank accounts, sell property, or manage estate assets. This guide explains everything you need to know.What Are Letters Testamentary?Letters Testamentary (Form DE-150) are an official court document that proves you have legal authority to act on behalf of the estate. They're issued by the probate court after the judge signs the Order for Probate appointing you as executor.Think of them as your "golden ticket"—the document that allows you to:Access and close the decedent's bank accountsSell real estate owned by the estateTransfer vehicle titlesManage investment and brokerage accountsFile tax returns for the estatePay creditors and estate expensesLetters Testamentary vs Letters of AdministrationYou'll hear two terms used:Letters TestamentaryIssued when there is a Will and the person is named as "Executor" in the Will.Letters of AdministrationIssued when there is no Will (intestate) and the person is appointed as "Administrator."Both documents grant the same legal authority—the only difference is the title (Executor vs Administrator) based on whether there's a Will.How to Get Letters TestamentaryHere's the process to obtain Letters:1File Petition for ProbateSubmit Form DE-111 to the Superior Court requesting appointment as executor.2Complete Required NoticesMail notice to heirs (DE-120) and publish in a newspaper.3Attend Probate HearingAppear at the scheduled hearing (or have your attorney appear). The judge signs the Order for Probate.4Request Certified CopiesOrder multiple certified copies of the Letters from the court clerk. You'll need them.How Many Certified Copies Do You Need?Order at least 5-10 certified copies. Many institutions require original certified copies and won't return them. Here's why you need so many:•Each bank may require its own copy•Title companies require a copy for each real estate transaction•The DMV needs a copy to transfer vehicle titles•Investment companies typically keep the copy you provide•Keep 1-2 copies for your recordsImportant: Certification Date MattersSome institutions require Letters certified within 60 days. If your Letters are older, you may need to get fresh certified copies from the court.Using Letters with Banks & Financial InstitutionsWhen you visit a bank with Letters Testamentary, you typically need:Certified copy of Letters TestamentaryCertified copy of the Death CertificateYour personal identification (driver's license)Bank's estate account application (they'll provide this)Most banks will open an "Estate Account" where you can consolidate the decedent's funds. This keeps estate money separate from your personal funds—which is legally required.Using Letters to Sell Real EstateTo sell property owned by the estate, the title company will require:Certified Letters Testamentary (recent certification)Proof that you have Independent Administration powers (if applicable)Court confirmation of sale (if you don't have Independent Administration)MyProbateCA Makes It EasyOur $3,995 flat fee includes:Preparation of all documents needed to obtain LettersGuidance on how many certified copies to orderInstructions for using Letters with banks and institutionsAttorney appearance at hearing if needed ($500 additional)Ready to get your Letters Testamentary? articles.title: Probate Bond Requirements in California: When You Need One
articles.text: One of the most confusing aspects of California probate is the probate bond requirement. This guide explains when bonds are required, how much they cost, and how to potentially avoid them altogether.What is a Probate Bond?A probate bond (also called an "executor bond" or "fiduciary bond") is a type of insurance policy that protects the estate's beneficiaries. If the executor mismanages estate funds or commits fraud, the bond company pays the beneficiaries up to the bond amount.Think of it as protection for the heirs—if something goes wrong, they have financial recourse through the bond company.When is a Bond Required?Under California Probate Code Section 8480, a bond is generally required unless one of the following exceptions applies:Bond Required• Will doesn't waive bond• No will (intestate)• Not all beneficiaries waive bond• Court has concerns about executorBond May Be Waived• Will specifically waives bond• All beneficiaries consent to waiver• Executor is sole beneficiary• Estate has limited assetsHow Much Does a Probate Bond Cost?The bond amount is typically set at the value of the estate's personal property plus one year's estimated income. The executor doesn't pay the full bond amount—they pay an annual premium to a surety company.Bond AmountAnnual Premium (0.5-1%)$100,000$500 - $1,000/year$250,000$1,250 - $2,500/year$500,000$2,500 - $5,000/year$1,000,000$5,000 - $10,000/yearImportant: Premium Paid from EstateThe bond premium is paid from estate funds, not the executor's personal money. However, it reduces the amount available for distribution to beneficiaries.How to Get a Bond WaiverThere are several ways to avoid the bond requirement:1Will WaiverThe best scenario: If the Will contains language like "I direct that no bond be required of my executor," the court will typically honor this.2Beneficiary ConsentAll beneficiaries can sign a written waiver agreeing that no bond is required. This is filed with the court.3Blocked AccountPlace estate funds in a "blocked account" that requires court permission to access. This protects funds without requiring a bond.4Limited AuthorityRequest appointment with limited powers (no IAEA) which may reduce or eliminate bond requirements.How the Bond Amount is CalculatedThe court calculates the required bond amount using this formula:Personal Property Value + Estimated Annual Income = Bond AmountReal property is generally not included in the bond calculation unless the executor has the power to sell it without court confirmation (IAEA powers).Getting Approved for a Probate BondSurety companies will evaluate the proposed executor before issuing a bond. They typically consider:Credit history - Good credit makes approval easierCriminal background - No felonies or financial crimesFinancial stability - Ability to manage estate responsiblyRelationship to decedent - Family members generally preferredWhat if You Can't Get a Bond?If you're unable to obtain a bond (due to poor credit or other issues), you have options:•Request a blocked account instead of a bond•Have a co-executor who can qualify for the bond•Step aside and let another qualified person serve as executor•Petition the court for waiver with supporting documentationWhen is the Bond Released?The bond remains in effect until the estate is fully administered and the executor is discharged by the court. This happens when:All debts and taxes have been paidAll assets have been distributed to beneficiariesFinal accounting has been approved by the courtOrder for Final Distribution has been signedHow MyProbateCA Helps with BondsOur $3,995 flat fee includes assistance with bond requirements:We determine if a bond is required for your caseWe help prepare bond waiver requests when applicableWe can recommend reliable surety companiesWe handle blocked account arrangements if neededKey Takeaways1Probate bonds protect beneficiaries, not the executor2Premium costs 0.5-1% of the bond amount annually3Bonds can often be waived if the Will allows or beneficiaries consent4Blocked accounts are an alternative to posting bondHave questions about bond requirements for your case? Start with MyProbateCA and we'll help determine if a bond is needed and how to minimize costs.Rozsa Gyene, Esq.California State Bar #208356 • 26+ Years ExperienceRozsa Gyene specializes in California probate administration, with extensive experience at the Stanley Mosk Courthouse in Los Angeles.Verify License Need Help With Your Probate Case?Get attorney oversight for a flat $3,995 fee—save $19,000+ compared to statutory fees.Explore Our Probate Services→ How Our Process Works→ Probate FAQ (50+ Questions)→ 35 California Locations→ Los Angeles Probate→ San Francisco Probate→ San Diego ProbateRelated ArticlesForms & DocumentsLetters Testamentary California GuideFees & CostsCalifornia Probate Fees ExplainedProcessWhat is a Probate Referee?Back to Learning Center

articles.title: How to File Probate in California: Step-by-Step Guide
articles.text: Filing probate in California can seem overwhelming, but it follows a predictable 11-phase process. This guide walks you through exactly what you need to do, from gathering documents to receiving your Letters Testamentary.Before You StartCalifornia probate is required when someone dies owning assets titled solely in their name worth more than $184,500 (or any real estate not in a trust). If the estate qualifies, you may be able to use a Small Estate Affidavit instead.Step 1: Gather Essential DocumentsBefore filing anything with the court, collect these critical documents:Original Will (if one exists) — the court requires the original, not a copyCertified Death Certificates — order 10-15 copies from the county recorderList of Assets — real estate, bank accounts, investments, vehiclesList of Heirs — names, addresses, and relationships of all beneficiaries and legal heirsList of Debts — mortgages, credit cards, medical bills, taxes owedStep 2: Determine Where to FileCalifornia probate must be filed in the Superior Court of the county where the decedent lived at the time of death (their "domicile"). This is true even if they owned property in other counties.Common California Probate CourtsLos Angeles County: Stanley Mosk Courthouse, 111 N. Hill StreetOrange County: Lamoreaux Justice Center, 341 The City DriveSan Diego County: Central Courthouse, 1100 Union StreetSan Francisco: Civic Center Courthouse, 400 McAllister StreetSanta Clara County: Downtown Superior Court, 191 N. First StreetSee all 35 California probate court locations →Step 3: Complete the Petition for Probate (Form DE-111)The Petition for Probate is your formal request to open the estate. This form requires:• Decedent's full legal name and any aliases• Date and place of death• Whether a will exists (and attach it)• Names and addresses of all heirs and beneficiaries• Estimated value of the estate• Name of proposed executor/administrator• Request for authority (full or limited)Common MistakeMany self-filed petitions are rejected because the heir information is incomplete or inconsistent. Every heir must be listed with their exact legal relationship to the decedent.Step 4: File with the Court and Pay FeesSubmit your completed petition to the probate clerk. You'll need to pay the filing fee at this time.California Probate Filing CostsPetition Filing Fee$435 - $500Newspaper Publication$200 - $350Certified Copies (each)$25 - $50Probate Referee Fee0.1% of assetsSee complete fee breakdown →Step 5: Publish Notice and Mail to HeirsCalifornia law requires two types of notice before the hearing:Newspaper PublicationPublish "Notice of Petition to Administer Estate" in an adjudicated newspaper for 3 consecutive weeks. The newspaper must be in the city where the decedent lived.Mail Notice (DE-120/121)Mail notice to all heirs, beneficiaries, and any creditors you know about at least 15 days before the hearing date.Step 6: Attend the Probate HearingApproximately 6-10 weeks after filing, you'll have your first court hearing. If filing in Los Angeles County, check for IGN notes 5-10 days before your hearing and file any required supplements.At the hearing, the judge will:• Review your petition for completeness• Confirm proper notice was given• Hear any objections from heirs or creditors• Appoint you as executor/administrator (if approved)• Issue Letters Testamentary or Letters of AdministrationStep 7: After Your Hearing - What's NextOnce appointed, you'll need to complete these remaining phases:7Inventory & AppraisalWork with the court-appointed probate referee to value all estate assets within 4 months.8Creditor ManagementNotice known creditors and wait the 4-month claim period before paying valid debts.9Tax ReturnsFile the decedent's final personal tax return and estate income tax returns if needed.10Final AccountingPrepare a detailed accounting of all money received and paid by the estate.11Final DistributionObtain court approval and distribute remaining assets to beneficiaries.Need Help Filing?MyProbateCA handles all 11 phases of California probate for a flat fee of $3,995 — saving you $19,000+ compared to statutory attorney fees. We prepare all documents, clear IGN notes, and guide you through every step.Start Your Case - FreeHow Long Does California Probate Take?Most California probate cases take 9 to 18 months from filing to final distribution. See our detailed timeline guide for what to expect each month.Timeline FactorsSimple estates: 9-12 months | Complex estates or disputes: 18-24+ monthsRozsa Gyene, Esq.California State Bar #208356 • 26+ Years ExperienceRozsa Gyene specializes in California probate administration, with extensive experience at the Stanley Mosk Courthouse in Los Angeles.Verify License Need Help With Your Probate Case?Get attorney oversight for a flat $3,995 fee—save $19,000+ compared to statutory fees.Explore Our Probate Services→ How Our Process Works→ Probate FAQ (50+ Questions)→ 35 California Locations→ Los Angeles Probate→ San Francisco Probate→ San Diego ProbateRelated ArticlesFees & CostsCalifornia Probate Fees: Statutory vs Flat FeeForms & DocumentsLetters Testamentary California GuideProcessProbate Timeline California: What to ExpectBack to Learning Center

articles.title: Small Estate Affidavit California: When You Don't Need Probate
articles.text: Not every estate needs to go through California's lengthy probate process. If the estate is small enough, you may be able to transfer assets using a Small Estate Affidavit — a simple form that avoids court entirely.Good NewsCalifornia has some of the most generous small estate thresholds in the country. As of April 1, 2022, you can transfer up to $184,500 in personal property without probate.What is a Small Estate Affidavit?A Small Estate Affidavit (also called a "Declaration for Collection of Personal Property") is a legal document that allows you to claim a deceased person's assets without going through probate court. Under California Probate Code Section 13100, qualifying successors can use this affidavit to:Collect bank account fundsTransfer vehicle titlesClaim stocks, bonds, and investment accountsCollect insurance proceeds payable to the estateRetrieve personal property from storage units or safe deposit boxesCalifornia Small Estate Limits (2024-2025)Current ThresholdsPersonal Property Affidavit(No court filing required)$184,500Simplified Real Property Petition(Streamlined court process)$184,500Spousal Property Petition(For surviving spouses)No LimitNote: Effective April 1, 2025, these limits increase to $208,850 for personal property and $750,000 for real property (primary residence only).Do You Qualify? Requirements ChecklistTo use a Small Estate Affidavit in California, ALL of the following must be true:40 Days Have PassedAt least 40 days must have elapsed since the decedent's deathNo Probate FiledNo probate proceeding is currently pending or has been conductedUnder the LimitTotal value of ALL estate property in California is $184,500 or lessYou're the Rightful SuccessorYou are entitled to the property under the will or California intestacy lawsNo Real Estate (for Affidavit)The estate does not include real property (separate process required)What DOESN'T Count Toward the $184,500 LimitGood news — many assets are excluded when calculating whether you're under the limit:Excluded from Calculation• Joint tenancy property• Property in a living trust• Life insurance (with named beneficiary)• Retirement accounts (401k, IRA with beneficiary)• Payable-on-death bank accounts• Transfer-on-death securities• Vehicles under $184,500 (with DMV affidavit)Included in Calculation• Bank accounts in decedent's name only• Stocks/bonds without TOD designation• Personal property (furniture, jewelry)• Vehicles titled solely in decedent's name• Business interests• Money owed to decedentHow to Use a Small Estate Affidavit: Step by StepStep 1: Wait 40 DaysYou cannot use the affidavit until 40 days after the date of death.Step 2: Prepare the AffidavitComplete the "Declaration for Collection of Personal Property" form. Include your information, the decedent's information, description of property, and your legal basis to claim it.Step 3: Attach Required DocumentsInclude a certified copy of the death certificate. If there's a will, attach a copy.Step 4: Sign Under Penalty of PerjuryThe affidavit must be signed and dated. Some institutions require notarization.Step 5: Present to the InstitutionDeliver the affidavit to the bank, brokerage, or other entity holding the property. They must release it within a reasonable time.Important WarningBy signing the affidavit, you become personally liable to creditors, other heirs, and the state of California if you misrepresent the facts or misuse the funds. This is a sworn statement under penalty of perjury.What About Real Estate?Real property (homes, land, commercial buildings) cannot be transferred with a Small Estate Affidavit. However, California offers a simplified process for small real estate holdings:Affidavit for Real Property of Small ValueIf the gross value of all real property in California is $184,500 or less (increasing to $750,000 for primary residences on April 1, 2025), you can file a simplified petition with the court. This is faster and cheaper than full probate.Requirements: 6 months must pass after death, no probate pending, property value under threshold.Small Estate Affidavit vs Full ProbateFactorSmall Estate AffidavitFull ProbateTime Required40 days + processing9-18 monthsCourt FilingNot requiredRequiredAttorney RequiredNoHighly recommendedCost$0 - $100$3,995 - $23,000+Asset Limit$184,500No limitWhen You Can't Avoid ProbateUnfortunately, a Small Estate Affidavit won't work if:Estate value exceeds $184,500Real estate is involved (unless using simplified real property petition)There are disputes among heirsCreditors need formal court processThe institution refuses to honor the affidavitEstate Over the Limit?If the estate exceeds $184,500 or includes real property, you'll need to file probate. articles.title: Probate Timeline California: What to Expect Each Month | MyProbateCA
articles.text: Quick Summary: California Probate Timeline•Simple estates: 9-12 months minimum•Average estates: 12-18 months•Complex estates: 18-36+ months•Mandatory minimum: 4-month creditor period (cannot be shortened)Overview: How Long Does Probate Take in California?California probate typically takes between 9 and 18 months for most estates. However, this timeline can vary significantly based on the complexity of the estate, whether there are disputes, and the efficiency of the local probate court.One thing that cannot change is California's mandatory 4-month creditor notification period. This waiting period is required by law (California Probate Code Section 9100) and gives creditors time to file claims against the estate. Even the simplest estate cannot close before this period ends.Understanding the probate timeline helps executors and beneficiaries set realistic expectations and plan accordingly. While you can't eliminate the waiting periods, working with an experienced probate attorney familiar with your local court can help minimize unnecessary delays.Important: If the estate qualifies for a small estate affidavit (under $184,500 in assets), you may be able to avoid probate entirely and transfer assets in as little as 40 days after death.Month-by-Month California Probate TimelineBelow is a detailed breakdown of what typically happens during each phase of California probate. Keep in mind that these timeframes can overlap and may vary based on your specific situation.Initial Filing & PetitionMonth 1Locate and review the original willIdentify heirs and beneficiariesInventory assets for the petitionFile Petition for Probate with the Superior CourtPay filing fees ($435-$550 depending on county)Schedule hearing date (typically 30-45 days out)Pro Tip: File the petition within 30 days of death to avoid potential complications.Notice & PublicationMonth 2Mail Notice of Petition to all heirs and beneficiariesPublish Notice of Death in local newspaper (3 consecutive weeks)File Proof of Service with the courtPrepare for probate hearingPro Tip: Use a newspaper approved for legal notices in the county where the decedent lived.Probate Hearing & AppointmentMonth 2-3Attend the probate hearingPresent will for admission to probateReceive court order appointing executor/administratorObtain Letters Testamentary or Letters of AdministrationOrder certified copies of Letters (typically 6-10 copies needed)Pro Tip: Letters Testamentary are essential - you'll need them to access bank accounts and manage assets.Asset Collection & NotificationMonths 3-4Open estate bank accountTransfer assets into estate nameNotify Social Security, pension providers, insurance companiesSend formal Notice to CreditorsBegin collecting debts owed to the estateSecure and insure real propertyPro Tip: Keep detailed records of all transactions - you'll need them for the final accounting.4-Month Creditor Period (Mandatory)Months 4-7Wait for creditor claims (4-month minimum period)Review and evaluate any claims receivedPay valid creditor claims from estate fundsReject invalid or excessive claimsContinue managing estate assetsFile federal estate tax return if required (due 9 months after death)Pro Tip: This waiting period cannot be shortened - it's required by California law.Real Property Sale (If Applicable)Months 5-8Obtain property appraisalList property for saleReview and accept offersFile Notice of Proposed Action (if selling below appraisal)Obtain court confirmation if requiredComplete sale and deposit proceeds into estate accountPro Tip: Sales at 90% or more of appraised value typically don't require court confirmation.Final Inventory & Tax ReturnsMonths 8-12Complete Inventory and Appraisal (Form DE-160)File final income tax returns for decedentFile estate income tax returns if applicablePay any outstanding taxesObtain tax clearance from FTB and IRS if neededPro Tip: Hire a CPA experienced with estate taxation to ensure compliance and minimize taxes.Final Accounting & PetitionMonths 10-15Prepare detailed accounting of all receipts and disbursementsCalculate statutory fees for executor and attorneyPrepare proposed distribution planFile Petition for Final DistributionMail notice to all interested partiesSchedule final hearingPro Tip: Accurate accounting is crucial - errors can delay distribution by months.Distribution & ClosingMonths 12-18Attend final hearing for court approvalReceive Order for Final DistributionDistribute assets to beneficiariesObtain receipts from all beneficiariesFile final receipts with the courtReceive Order Discharging ExecutorPro Tip: Keep copies of all signed receipts - they protect you from future claims.Common Causes of Probate DelaysWhile the timeline above represents a typical probate case, several factors can significantly extend the process. Being aware of these potential delays can help you plan and potentially avoid them.Will Contests+6-24+ monthsIf someone challenges the validity of the will, probate essentially pauses until the dispute is resolved through mediation, settlement, or trial.Missing Heirs+3-12 monthsIf beneficiaries cannot be located, the court may require extensive search efforts and publication before proceeding.Real Property Issues+3-6 monthsClouded titles, boundary disputes, or difficulties selling property can significantly extend the timeline.Tax Complications+3-12 monthsComplex tax situations, audits, or disputes with tax authorities can delay final distribution.Creditor Disputes+2-6 monthsIf creditors file claims that must be litigated, resolution can take several additional months.Court Backlogs+1-4 monthsSome California counties have significant court backlogs, especially in larger urban areas like Los Angeles.How to Speed Up the Probate ProcessWhile you cannot eliminate the mandatory waiting periods, there are several strategies to minimize delays and keep your probate case moving efficiently.1File PromptlyDon't delay starting the process. File the petition within 30 days of death to get your hearing date scheduled as soon as possible. Learn more in our step-by-step filing guide.2Hire an Experienced Probate AttorneyAn attorney who regularly practices in your specific court knows the local rules, judges' preferences, and how to avoid common mistakes that cause delays. Our flat-fee probate service handles all 11 phases efficiently.3Organize Documents EarlyGather all necessary documents before filing: death certificate, original will, asset statements, beneficiary information, and creditor details. Missing documents cause delays.4Respond Quickly to Court RequestsWhen the court requests additional information or documents, respond immediately. Delays in responding can push your case to the back of the queue.5Communicate with BeneficiariesKeep all heirs and beneficiaries informed throughout the process. Clear communication can prevent disputes and objections that delay distribution.6Handle Real Property StrategicallyIf selling real estate, list it early in the process. Sales at or above 90% of appraised value don't require court confirmation, which saves significant time.Visual Probate Timeline Overview1FilingMonth 12HearingMonth 2-33Creditor Period4 Months (Required)4AccountingMonth 8-125DistributionMonth 12-18Total Timeline: 9-18 months (typical) | 18-36+ months (complex estates)Frequently Asked Questions About Probate TimelineHow long does probate take in California?California probate typically takes 9 to 18 months for straightforward estates. Complex estates with disputes, real property sales, or creditor issues may take 2 years or longer. The mandatory 4-month creditor period means no probate can close in less than about 7-8 months at absolute minimum.What is the mandatory 4-month creditor period in California probate?California law requires a minimum 4-month waiting period after Letters Testamentary are issued, during which creditors can file claims against the estate. This period cannot be shortened and is designed to protect creditors' rights.Can probate be expedited in California?While the 4-month creditor period cannot be shortened, you can speed up other phases by filing documents promptly, responding quickly to court requests, and working with experienced probate attorneys who know the local court procedures. Some courts also offer expedited hearing dates in certain circumstances.What happens if probate takes longer than expected?If probate extends beyond initial expectations, beneficiaries must wait for their inheritances. The executor continues to manage the estate and may need to file status reports with the court. In some cases, the executor can request permission to make partial distributions to beneficiaries while the case is pending.How much does probate cost for an 18-month case?California statutory probate fees are based on estate value, not duration. However, longer cases may incur additional "extraordinary fees" for complex matters. Our flat-fee service of $3,995 covers all standard probate work regardless of how long the case takes.Need Help Navigating the Probate Timeline?Our experienced team handles California probate cases every day. We know how to keep your case moving efficiently through each phase, minimizing delays and reducing stress.Schedule Free ConsultationCall 818-337-4071Related ArticlesHow to File Probate in CaliforniaStep-by-step guide to starting the probate process.Small Estate Affidavit CaliforniaLearn when you can skip probate entirely.Letters Testamentary GuideEssential document for managing estate assets.Rozsa Gyene, Esq.California State Bar #208356 • 26+ Years ExperienceRozsa Gyene specializes in California probate administration, with extensive experience at the Stanley Mosk Courthouse in Los Angeles.Verify License Need Help With Your Probate Case?Get attorney oversight for a flat $3,995 fee—save $19,000+ compared to statutory fees.Explore Our Probate Services→ How Our Process Works→ Probate FAQ (50+ Questions)→ 35 California Locations→ Los Angeles Probate→ San Francisco Probate→ San Diego ProbateBack to Learning Center

articles.title: What Happens If You Die Without a Will in California? Intestate Succession Explained
articles.text: When someone dies without a valid will in California, their estate doesn't simply go to whoever wants it. Instead, California's intestate succession laws dictate exactly who inherits — and the results often surprise families.Common MisconceptionMany people believe that dying without a will means "the state takes everything." This is almost never true. California has a detailed system for distributing assets to relatives — the state only inherits when absolutely no family can be found.What is Intestate Succession?"Intestate" means dying without a valid will. When this happens, California Probate Code Section 6400 and subsequent sections determine who inherits. This body of law is called intestate succession.The rules create a strict hierarchy of inheritance based on family relationships. Your closest relatives inherit first, and more distant relatives only inherit if closer relatives don't exist.Who Inherits Under California Intestate Succession?The distribution depends on your family situation. Here's how California law prioritizes heirs:If You're Married (With or Without Children)California distinguishes between community property and separate property:Community PropertyProperty acquired during marriage100% goes to surviving spouseSeparate PropertyProperty owned before marriage or received as gift/inheritanceSplit depends on children/relatives (see table below)Separate Property DistributionFamily SituationSpouse ReceivesOthers ReceiveSpouse + 1 child1/2Child gets 1/2Spouse + 2+ children1/3Children share 2/3 equallySpouse + no children, but parents1/2Parents get 1/2Spouse + no children, but siblings1/2Siblings share 1/2Spouse only (no children, parents, or siblings)100%—If You're NOT MarriedWithout a spouse, inheritance follows this order:1Children (and descendants of deceased children)Divided equally among children. If a child died, their children inherit their share.2ParentsIf no children, parents inherit equally (or surviving parent gets all).3Siblings (and descendants of deceased siblings)If no children or parents, siblings share equally.4Grandparents, aunts, uncles, cousinsThe law continues through increasingly distant relatives.∞State of California (Escheat)Only if absolutely no relatives can be found after diligent search.Important Rules to KnowHalf-Relatives Inherit EquallyHalf-siblings are treated the same as full siblings under California law.Adopted Children Have Full RightsLegally adopted children inherit exactly like biological children.Stepchildren Do NOT InheritUnless legally adopted, stepchildren have no inheritance rights under intestate succession.Unmarried Partners Inherit NOTHINGDomestic partners registered with the state are treated like spouses, but unmarried couples have zero inheritance rights.Do You Still Need Probate Without a Will?Yes — Probate is Still RequiredA common myth is that having no will means no probate. In reality, intestate estates almost always require probate, and the process is often more complicated because:The court must determine who the rightful heirs areAn administrator must be appointed (instead of an executor named in a will)A probate bond is usually required (often waived when there's a will)Finding and notifying all potential heirs takes more timeWhat Assets Pass Outside of Intestate Succession?Not all assets are distributed through intestate succession. These assets pass directly to named beneficiaries:Pass to Named Beneficiaries• Life insurance policies• Retirement accounts (401k, IRA)• Payable-on-death bank accounts• Transfer-on-death securities• Property in a living trust• Joint tenancy propertySubject to Intestate Succession• Bank accounts in decedent's name only• Real estate in decedent's name only• Vehicles titled solely to decedent• Personal property (furniture, jewelry)• Business interests• Investment accounts without TODReal-World ExampleScenario: John dies without a willJohn was married to Maria and had two adult children from a previous marriage. His estate includes:• Family home (community property with Maria): $800,000• Inheritance from his mother (separate property): $300,000• 401(k) with Maria as beneficiary: $200,000How it's distributed:• Family home: 100% to Maria (community property)• 401(k): 100% to Maria (named beneficiary)• $300,000 inheritance: Maria gets 1/3 ($100,000), children split 2/3 ($100,000 each)Frequently Asked QuestionsWhat if the deceased was separated but not divorced?Legally, they're still married. The separated spouse has full inheritance rights under intestate succession until the divorce is finalized.Can I inherit if I killed the deceased?No. California's "slayer statute" (Probate Code § 250) prevents anyone who feloniously kills the decedent from inheriting from them.What about children born outside of marriage?They have full inheritance rights as long as paternity was legally established (through acknowledgment, court order, or genetic testing).How long does intestate probate take?Typically 12-18 months — sometimes longer if heir identification is complicated. See our probate timeline guide for details.Need Help With an Intestate Estate?Administering an estate without a will can be complicated. articles.title: Executor Duties in California Probate: Complete Responsibilities Guide
articles.text: Being named executor of a California estate is both an honor and a significant responsibility. As executor (also called "personal representative"), you're legally obligated to manage the estate, protect its assets, pay debts, and distribute property to beneficiaries — all while navigating California's probate court system.Executor vs. AdministratorAn executor is named in a will. An administrator is appointed by the court when there's no will or the named executor can't serve. The duties are essentially identical — only the appointment process differs.Your Core Fiduciary DutiesAs executor, you have a fiduciary duty to the estate and its beneficiaries. This is the highest legal duty of care and means you must:Duty of LoyaltyAct solely in the interest of the beneficiaries, never for personal gain. Avoid conflicts of interest.Duty of CareManage estate assets prudently. Make informed decisions. Seek professional help when needed.Duty to AccountKeep detailed records of all transactions. Provide accountings to the court and beneficiaries.Duty of ImpartialityTreat all beneficiaries fairly. Don't favor one heir over another unless the will specifies.Complete Executor Responsibilities Checklist1Immediate Actions (First 30 Days)Locate the original willCheck safe deposit boxes, home safes, the decedent's attorney, or the county clerk.Obtain 10-15 certified death certificatesYou'll need these for banks, title companies, insurance, and government agencies.Secure all estate propertyChange locks if needed, collect valuables, redirect mail, secure vehicles.Notify Social Security, pension providers, employersStop benefits to avoid overpayments that must be repaid.Contact a probate attorneyGet guidance on whether probate is needed and understand the process.2Opening Probate (Months 1-2)File Petition for Probate (Form DE-111)Submit to the Superior Court in the county where the decedent lived.Post probate bond (if required)May be waived if the will includes "full IAEA" powers.Notify heirs and beneficiariesMail Notice of Petition (Form DE-121) at least 15 days before hearing.Publish notice in local newspaperRequired for 3 consecutive weeks to notify unknown creditors.Attend probate hearingThe court will formally appoint you and issue Letters Testamentary.3Estate Administration (Months 2-12)Open estate bank accountDeposit estate funds here. Never commingle with personal funds.Inventory all assetsCreate a complete list of real property, bank accounts, investments, personal property.Work with probate referee for appraisalsThe court-appointed referee values most non-cash assets.File Inventory and Appraisal (Form DE-160)Due within 4 months of appointment.Notify known creditorsMail Notice to Creditors (Form DE-157) within 30 days of appointment.Review and pay valid creditor claimsCreditors have 4 months to file claims. Evaluate each claim carefully.Manage ongoing expensesPay mortgage, utilities, insurance, property taxes from estate funds.File tax returnsFinal personal return (Form 1040), estate income tax (Form 1041), and estate tax (Form 706) if applicable.4Closing the Estate (Final Months)Prepare final accountingDocument all receipts, disbursements, and distributions.File Petition for Final DistributionRequest court approval to distribute remaining assets to beneficiaries.Distribute assets to beneficiariesTransfer property, write checks, and obtain receipts from each beneficiary.File receipts with courtProve that beneficiaries received their distributions.Request discharge from dutiesThe court officially releases you from your executor role.Executor Compensation in CaliforniaUnder California Probate Code Section 10800, executors are entitled to statutory compensation:Statutory Executor FeesFirst $100,000 of estate value4%Next $100,0003%Next $800,0002%Next $9,000,0001%Above $10,000,0000.5%Example: For a $500,000 estate: $4,000 + $3,000 + $6,000 = $13,000 executor feeExecutor Fees Are Taxable IncomeUnlike inheritances (which are tax-free), executor compensation is taxable as ordinary income. Many family member executors choose to waive fees, especially if they're also beneficiaries.Personal Liability RisksExecutors can be held personally liable for:Mismanaging assets — Letting property deteriorate, making bad investments, or losing estate fundsPremature distributions — Distributing assets before paying all debts and taxesMissing tax deadlines — Failing to file returns or pay taxes on timeSelf-dealing — Using estate assets for personal benefitIgnoring creditors — Distributing assets without properly addressing valid claimsProtect YourselfThe best way to avoid liability is to: (1) keep meticulous records, (2) get court approval before major decisions, (3) work with a probate attorney, and (4) never commingle estate funds with personal funds.Frequently Asked QuestionsCan I decline to be an executor?Yes. Being named in a will doesn't obligate you to serve. You can renounce (decline) before the court appoints you. Once appointed, you can petition to resign, but the court must approve.Can there be multiple executors?Yes. Co-executors must generally act together and agree on decisions. This can provide checks and balances but may also create conflict. Each co-executor is entitled to full statutory compensation.Can an executor also be a beneficiary?Absolutely. It's very common for a spouse or child to serve as both executor and primary beneficiary. However, you must still fulfill all duties impartially and document everything carefully.What if beneficiaries disagree with my decisions?Beneficiaries can file objections with the probate court. The court will review your actions and determine if they were appropriate. Always document your reasoning for major decisions.How long does probate take?California probate typically takes 9-18 months. See our complete probate timeline guide for month-by-month details.Overwhelmed by Executor Duties?You don't have to do this alone. Our experienced probate attorneys guide executors through every step of the process for a flat fee of $3,995. We handle the paperwork, court filings, and deadlines — you focus on your family.Get Executor Support TodayRozsa Gyene, Esq.California State Bar #208356 • 26+ Years ExperienceRozsa Gyene specializes in California probate administration, with extensive experience at the Stanley Mosk Courthouse in Los Angeles.Verify License Need Help With Your Probate Case?Get attorney oversight for a flat $3,995 fee—save $19,000+ compared to statutory fees.Explore Our Probate Services→ How Our Process Works→ Probate FAQ (50+ Questions)→ 35 California Locations→ Los Angeles Probate→ San Francisco Probate→ San Diego ProbateRelated ArticlesStep-by-Step GuideHow to File Probate in CaliforniaExecutor GuideProbate Bond Requirements CaliforniaForms & DocumentsLetters Testamentary California GuideBack to Learning Center
